newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's anti-rebel fight straining jails, courts.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's anti-rebel fight straining jails, courts.

text.p: Turkey's struggle to combat rebel groups is placing an increasing strain on the country's prisons and legal system, the Justice Ministry said on Monday.
"The strong increase in the number of detainees at (special) 'terror prisons', particularly in (the southeastern city of) Diyarbakir and Istanbul is creating trouble," the ministry said.

In a statement issued during a budget commission meeting, it said the dormitory system in Turkey's prisons encouraged violent uprisings and hunger strikes and was enabling extremist groups to spread their influence throughout the system.

In July, 12 leftist inmates starved themselves to death in a campaign to end maltreatment and improve prisoners' access to families and lawyers. The government subsequently committed itself to improving prison conditions.
Since then over 100 inmates have begun a hunger strike at a prison in the western town of Aydin to protest at conditions.

A spokeswoman from Turkey's Human Rights Association told Reuters the protest, by prisoners linked to the separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), had entered its 47th day. She said 18 of the 102 protesters were near death.
Hunger strikes in Konya and Amasya prisons ended on Monday after demands from improved conditions were met, she said.
The hunger strikes highlight the pressures on a prison system struggling to cope with a jail population totalling 54,292, in 562 jails. Of these, 28,989 prisoners have been convicted.
The number of inmates held in 58 special prisons for "terrorist activities" totals 9,234. Of these 5,475 have been convicted, the ministry statement said.
It said the burden of state security courts had also reached the stage where the existing 19 courts had become insufficient. It called for establishment of a further 26 courts.

Turkey's security forces have fought a 12-year battle against PKK rebels seeking self-rule in the southeast of the country. State authorities are also regularly targeted by far-left urban guerrilla groups.
